opus-5.5.text:
Well, when I started at OpenAI on leave from UT Austin, I was looking for some piece of the AI safety problem where a theoretical computer scientist could actually make a concrete contribution, and attribution turned out to be one of the clearest.

Once you have language models that can produce text indistinguishable from what a human would write, you get a whole range of misuses. The obvious one, which every professor I know is worried about, is academic cheating: students turning in essays they didn't write. But it goes well beyond that. There's propaganda and disinformation at scale: flooding comment sections or social media with millions of plausible-sounding posts that seem to come from real, distinct people. There's impersonating someone's writing style to frame them or to run a more convincing phishing scam. There's spam that's much harder to filter.

What all of these have in common is that the harm comes from deception about provenance. The text isn't necessarily bad in itself. The problem is that people are being misled about whether a human wrote it. So if you had a reliable way to say "this came from GPT," you'd defuse a large fraction of these misuses at once. That's what makes it feel central to me: one technical tool that addresses many different harms.

There are basically two approaches. One is to train a classifier to distinguish human-written text from AI-written text after the fact. That works to some extent, but it's an arms race and it produces false positives, and you really don't want to accuse a student of cheating because some discriminator didn't like their prose. The approach I worked on is watermarking. You take advantage of the fact that the model is already making random choices about which token to output next, and instead of using true randomness, you use a pseudorandom function keyed with a secret. To an ordinary reader the output looks exactly the same; you can even arrange it so there's provably no degradation in quality. But someone holding the key can compute a score over the text, and after a few hundred tokens you can get very high statistical confidence that it came from the model.

I should be honest about the limitations, because they're real. A watermark like this can be attacked. You can paraphrase the text with another model, or ask the model to write in some pattern and then strip it out afterward. It only helps if the companies running the most capable models actually deploy it, and open-source models are a separate problem. So I don't see it as a silver bullet. But I think it raises the cost of misuse a lot, especially for the lazy, high-volume cases, which are a big part of the problem. And I think it's something we should want in place before these models become even more capable and even more woven into how information flows through society.

r001.rationale: The response says that reliably identifying text as model-generated would defuse many misuses and that watermarking raises the cost of misuse.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd say it's central for a pretty simple reason: once you have models that can produce text indistinguishable from what a human would write, almost every misuse you can imagine runs through that. Students handing in essays they didn't write, sure, that's the one everyone talks about, but also mass-produced propaganda, fake product reviews, spam that evades filters, impersonation of real people. And then there's something that I think is underappreciated, which is the problem for AI research itself. If the internet fills up with model-generated text, and the next generation of models trains on the internet, you've got this feedback loop where the training data is contaminated and nobody can tell which parts came from a human.

When I went to OpenAI, this was actually the first problem I latched onto, partly because it felt like one where a theoretical computer scientist could contribute something. The question is: can you take a language model and have it embed a hidden statistical signal in its outputs, a watermark, that's invisible to a reader but that lets someone with a secret key verify, with high confidence, that this text came from the model? And it turns out you can do this without degrading the quality of the output at all, by exploiting the fact that the model is already sampling randomly at each token. You just make that randomness pseudorandom in a way you control. The key insight is that a language model normally has to choose among many plausible next words. Instead of flipping a fair coin, you flip a coin that's biased according to a function of the previous words and a secret key. Any individual choice still looks perfectly natural, but across a few hundred words the statistical signal becomes overwhelming.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. It's not a complete solution. Someone can paraphrase the text with a different model, or you can have a motivated adversary who gets around it. But I think of it as raising the cost of misuse, much like a lock on a door. And it addresses a question that I think is going to loom larger and larger over the next decade, which is simply: as more and more of what we read is generated by machines, do we have any way of knowing?

r001.rationale: The response explains that a watermark can identify model-generated text and says this raises the cost of misuse.

astra-6.text:
Well, as these models get better, we’re going to be in a world where you can produce enormous amounts of plausible-looking text at almost no cost. And that has wonderful applications, but it also creates problems: spam, impersonation, automated propaganda, students submitting work that they didn’t write. All of these raise the question of whether we can tell where a piece of text came from.

The tricky thing is that you don’t want your solution to depend on the model making mistakes. If your detector looks for awkward phrasing or factual errors, then it becomes less useful as the models improve. So the question that interests me is whether you can build some signal into the generation process itself—a watermark, for example—that doesn’t noticeably change the text for a reader, but that you can detect statistically if you know what to look for.

That wouldn’t solve every problem. Someone could rewrite the text, and not every model would use it. But it could give us one useful tool for establishing provenance, at a time when simply reading something and saying, ‘That sounds human,’ is becoming much less reliable.

r001.rationale: The response says text provenance could be established with a detectable watermark, but it does not state that distinguishing model-generated text would make misuse more difficult.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, as these systems get better, we’re going to live in a world where you can no longer tell, just by reading something, whether a human wrote it or an AI generated it. And that has implications for everything from students turning in essays to people producing spam or misinformation at an enormous scale.

The question is whether we can give people some way to establish where a piece of text came from. One approach that interests me is watermarking: making subtle statistical choices in the generated text that don’t noticeably affect its quality, but that someone with the right key could detect. You wouldn’t expect a reader to see anything unusual, yet there could be evidence that the text came from a particular AI system.

Of course, that’s not going to solve every problem. Someone could rewrite the text, or use a model that doesn’t include a watermark. But I think having some ability to identify AI-generated content is an important part of adapting to a world where generating convincing text becomes essentially free.

r001.rationale: The response says AI text may be hard to distinguish and gives spam and misinformation as misuse examples. It presents watermarking as a way to identify AI-generated content, but does not clearly state that distinguishing it would make misuse more difficult.
